item.title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP (178 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://kapteko.com/15-million-webservers/, See on Hacker News

Nov 18, 2026

Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldn’t get funding, so we’re bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, I’ll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and we’ll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.

Web server

Instead of vibe coding it all, let’s use an ancient technique called learning. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.

  1. listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket
  2. accept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socket
  3. recv - receives data from a socket
  4. send - sends data
  5. close - closes

What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Let’s use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.

int main(void)
{
    // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port
    int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); 
    if (listen(server, 128) < 0)
        return 1;
    const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK";
    for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }
}

It couldn’t be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that we’ve learned everything, let’s finish the article and call it a day:

$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done
...
...
28232
program exited with error 1

Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, we’ve run out of ports! We’re using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.

$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768    60999

Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.

  • Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).
  • Ports 1-1024 require root.
  • Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You don’t want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.
  • Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.

Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but that’s still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Let’s simply connect 15M/32k=450 new network cards to the server.

The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldn’t be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, we’ll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!

UPD. I’ve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didn’t get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Can’t we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?

Let’s use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. We’ll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:

// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it
int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]);
const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001;  // ex. 10.64.0.1
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i);  // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2

And now we can finally finish the article.

$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done
...
...
Out of memory

Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would take… 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.

Runtime

By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.

TLDR: We’re using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main process’s memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.

Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, we’re doomed to build another specialised runtime. Let’s get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?

Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. What’s the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Let’s take another look at the loop.

for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }

This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, we’d need to save the following state:

struct Context {
    pc: u64,        // Instruction address to return to
    fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor
    fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor
}

We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. We’re playing it safe here - we don’t need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?

$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?"
Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kb

Here’s what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.

  • 14M idle connections - 0 bytes
  • Scheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB
  • 1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GB

Only half of our RAM budget, yay! I don’t often exceed my own expectations. Let’s validate it:

int main(void) {
    // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing
    // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY!
    for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) {
        int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); 
        listen(server, 1)
    }
}
$ ./run_15m_idle_servers
Out Of Memory
$ dmesg | tail -n 1
'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?

Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. I’m not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, it’s too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - let’s dive into networking in the kernel.

Networking in the kernel

Remember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:

int main(void)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) {
        socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    }
}

That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Let’s ask AI where all the memory goes:

StructsizeofDescription
struct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeeping
struct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and padding
struct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socket
struct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeeping
Total3384B

Potato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesn’t look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. It’s Sunday and I have few tokens left, so we’ll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?

What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we can’t solve a task, we’re working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hm… level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!

The OSI model is… um… something I studied at university. Yeah, that’s a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, that’s exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?

Clear.

Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.

TCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkels’s Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.

There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:

  • gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stack
  • Seastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDB
  • lwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IP
  • F-Stack uses FreeBSD’s TCP/IP stack

Go, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but they’re nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So we’ll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:

>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for
>bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at all

So, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and can’t do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:

  • TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layer
  • TAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layer
  • DPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernel

smoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and they’re easy to use.

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() {
        Some("tun") => (
            TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?,
            Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip),
        ),
        Some("tap") => (
            TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?,
            Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()),
        ),
        _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"),
    };
    let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now());
    iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| {
        addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap();
    });
    let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new());
    
    // Main network loop
    loop {
        let now = Instant::now();
        iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets);
        wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?;
    }
}

But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: it’s common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.

DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and you’re done; when you want to read what you’ve received - it’s already there.

There’s another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but there’s a cost.

DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:

loop {
    send_from_app_memory_to_network();
    receive_from_network_to_app_memory();
}

There’s another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers can’t work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interface… it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, you’ll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.

Actually, there’s a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).

To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.

Now the final flow is:

  1. The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memory
  2. The runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by one
  3. Guest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adapters
  4. All 15M guests start listening, each on its own address
  5. The scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the next

And now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:

Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.

Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.

References

  • https://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers source
  • https://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDK
  • https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation site
  • https://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

Affected software

Your deployment

The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.

Framework Status on an affected Ruby
Rails Affected
Sinatra (classic style) Affected
Other frameworks and plain Rack Not exposed by default

Self-hosted software

The latest version of the following popular software bundles an affected Ruby.

Software Bundled Ruby Status
GitLab 19.6.0 3.3.13 Affected
GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 4.0.9 Affected
Mastodon 4.7.5 4.0.9 Affected
OpenProject 17.9.7 4.0.9 Affected
Discourse 2026.10.1 3.4.7 Affected
Chatwoot 4.20.0 3.4.4 Affected

Updated 19 November 2026 at 10:00 UTC.

Your deployment

Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.

Self-hosted software

Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products.

Technical details

Root cause

Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital ß. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).

The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each ß adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.

UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f.

Primitive

A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length.

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.

Proof of concept

We'll be publishing a proof of concept in a week, once people have had time to upgrade.

item.title: Gemini 4 Neon looks like an Opus 5.5 competitor (233 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://micjm.com/blog/gemini-4-neon-looks-like-a-top-model/, See on Hacker News

TLDR: we project Gemini 4 Neon’s performance based on what a faster Gemini 4 Carbon might score and find it equivalent to Opus 5.5

Gemini 4 Carbon is the best model on the Agent Duel leaderboard if you exclude early voting. Carbon’s main problem is that it is slooooow.

Today, Gemini 4 Neon was released, and looks to be an incremental benchmark improvement with a very large speed improvement. Earlier today, it was being served extremely fast via OpenRouter: 127 tokens per second. This is way faster than Carbon at 46 tokens per second.

This got me wondering, could Neon be not just a good model but the best model?

Modeling our leaderboard

To investigate, I modeled the win rate in our leaderboard. The best model has three components, model identity, speed and whether the user voted early. My initial modeling did poorly, so I added an interaction between speed and early voting. This ended up working well.

And surprisingly, speed seems to be pretty much as important as model identity (another blog on that soon).

Projecting Gemini 4 Neon performance

If you assume the same performance as Gemini 4 Carbon (which is reasonable given even better benchmark scores), and 127 tps, we would project an Elo on the Agent Duel leaderboard of 1,066, just below Opus 5.5 at 1,078 in our later analysis snapshot.

The 90% interval for the projected Elo difference between Gemini 4 Neon and Opus 5.5 is -94 to +68, with Neon projected to win 48.3% of the time against Opus (counting ties as half a win).

item.title: We need smart people who give a shit (642 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://violetpixel.com/blog/2026-11-17-we-need-smart-people-who-give-a-shit/, See on Hacker News

Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST

🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit

Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions.

When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable.

The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things:

  1. Intimate knowledge of the system
  2. The drive and determination to force the system to work

Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure.

Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse.

And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365, Air Traffic Control, United Airlines' systems, the NSA's network, many major banks, Apple's systems, and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI.

I guess that depends on how you look at it.

I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit.

So where did they go?

Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity.

Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea.

People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from?

It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics.

Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this.

It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real.

Thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system).

We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a big problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail.

I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now.

Unfortunately, we're all getting burned.

item.title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion (281 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2026/11/18/multiple-vulnerabilities-in-regexp-and-string/, See on Hacker News

Posted by mame on 18 Nov 2026

Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading.

CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers.

GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5: Heap buffer overflow in case conversion of strings

Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x: Double free in regular expression compilation

Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px: Integer overflow in case conversion of strings

Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r: Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive regular expression matching

Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way.

GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w: Heap buffer overflow in regular expression compilation

Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4: Heap buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s

Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s. Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h: Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive backreference matching

Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process.

Affected versions

  • Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier
  • Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12
  • Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9

Recommended action

We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14.

Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes.
