item.title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation (111 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://jimmyhmiller.com/magic-of-partial-evaluation, See on Hacker News

There are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful. It doesn't matter if they have any practical use. It doesn't matter that you will never convince your coworkers to consider them. There is just something captivating about the way some computational systems work.

For me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages. Programming languages are my obsession. I have never met a problem that couldn't be solved by introducing yet another programming language. Solving a problem at the programming language level is about solving the meta problem. Instead of trying to solve a particular problem, we take a step back and ask how we can solve a whole class of problems at once.

So when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole. One of these incredibly beautiful but tricky concepts goes by the name partial evaluation. If you are fascinated by interpreters and compilers, partial evaluation will teach you how they are related, and how you can get a compiler for free.

Partial Evaluation Easy Mode#

Partial evaluation has been a fascination of mine for a while. But this whole thing came up when James Long announced he had revived Meta's partial evaluator for JavaScript called prepack. When I first heard about prepack, I had some high hopes and expectations for the project, but was sadly let down. This revival brought to light those same dreams. But sadly, just as with the original aim, prepack was not designed for beauty, but for practicality. So I figured it was time to renew my own efforts.

Yes, in some ways this is a post repping my own library I'm releasing. But I'm not doing this because I want it to be used. I'm doing this because it lets you play with the idea I find so beautiful. That is what this post is about.

Doing Partial Evaluation by Hand#

Consider the following code:

function factorial(n) {
  if (n <= 1) return 1;
  return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

factorial(5);

As a person who reads code, you can think about how this code computes and what answer it will give. But you can do more than just give the answer. You can see the expanded form of this particular code for these particular calls. This code is spiritually the same as the following expression, once we expand it out.

5 * (4 * (3 * (2 * 1)))

In this case, there is really nothing at all that this code needs to do at runtime. A sufficiently smart compiler will just run this code directly at compile time and give the answer. But this is a bit less clear if things come in at runtime.

function power(base, exponent) {
  if (exponent === 0) return 1;
  return base * power(base, exponent - 1);
}

power(process.argv[2], 5)

It might seem like we can't do anything here, but again, if you are used to thinking about how programs run, you can trace this out and realize this is just the same as:

process.argv[2] * (process.argv[2] * (process.argv[2] * (process.argv[2] * (process.argv[2] * 1))))

What we have done in both of these cases is called partial evaluation. In the first, it was a trivial case because everything was statically known. But in this latter case, we have reduced a program down into the essentials of its dynamic structure. There are no recursive function calls left. All of this has been expanded as far as it could till we get just the dynamic parts of the code remaining.

The Big Idea#

This intuitive notion of partial evaluation is all you need to know to appreciate the beauty here. Partial evaluation just evaluates the part of the program we can evaluate at build time and leaves all the rest. When we do this with certain programs in certain combinations, we get some quite surprising, incredible behavior.

function calculate(expr) {
  if (typeof expr === "number") return expr;
  switch (expr[0]) {
    case "+": return calculate(expr[1]) + calculate(expr[2]);
    case "-": return calculate(expr[1]) - calculate(expr[2]);
    case "*": return calculate(expr[1]) * calculate(expr[2]);
    case "/": return calculate(expr[1]) / calculate(expr[2]);
    default: throw new Error("Unknown operator");
  }
}

calculate(["+", 1, ["*", 2, 3]]);

Here we have a very simple interpreter for a language that just supports arithmetic. For the above expression, you should be able to think about how we could start "partially" evaluating it. (In this case, it can be a full evaluation.) If this kind of partial evaluation isn't quite clicking for you, I've put the steps below to hopefully help it make sense.

calculate(["+", 1, ["*", 2, 3]])
→ calculate(1) + calculate(["*", 2, 3])
→ 1 + calculate(["*", 2, 3])
→ 1 + (calculate(2) * calculate(3))
→ 1 + (2 * calculate(3))
→ 1 + (2 * 3)
→ 1 + 6
→ 7

This is a simple evaluation of the code. But what happens if we throw a value we don't know into the expression?

calculate(["+", Number(process.argv[2]), ["*", 2, 3]])
→ calculate(Number(process.argv[2])) + calculate(["*", 2, 3])
→ Number(process.argv[2]) + calculate(["*", 2, 3])
→ Number(process.argv[2]) + (calculate(2) * calculate(3))
→ Number(process.argv[2]) + (2 * calculate(3))
→ Number(process.argv[2]) + (2 * 3)
→ Number(process.argv[2]) + 6

Here we can see that clear partial evaluation difference. We don't know how to evaluate Number(process.argv[2]). We have no idea what the answer to that will be. But as part of this process, we do know some partial information about it. For example, when we get to

if (typeof expr === "number") return expr;

we know that Number(process.argv[2]) is indeed a number. So we can partially evaluate it further. Hopefully this is all making sense. But if you are like me, this all might seem a bit trivial and uninteresting. So let's look at a more complicated example.

function brainfuck(code, input = "") {
  const tape = new Uint8Array(30000);
  const jumps = {}, stack = [];
  let pointer = 0, inputPointer = 0, output = "";
  for (let i = 0; i < code.length; i++) {
    if (code[i] === "[") stack.push(i);
    if (code[i] === "]") {
      const start = stack.pop();
      jumps[start] = i;
      jumps[i] = start;
    }
  }
  for (let i = 0; i < code.length; i++) {
    switch (code[i]) {
      case ">": pointer++; break;
      case "<": pointer--; break;
      case "+": tape[pointer]++; break;
      case "-": tape[pointer]--; break;
      case ".": output += String.fromCharCode(tape[pointer]); break;
      case ",":
        tape[pointer] = inputPointer < input.length
          ? input.charCodeAt(inputPointer++)
          : 0;
        break;
      case "[": if (!tape[pointer]) i = jumps[i]; break;
      case "]": if (tape[pointer]) i = jumps[i]; break;
    }
  }
  return output;
}

brainfuck("++++++++++[>+++++++>++++++++++>+++>+<<<<-]>++.>+.+++++++..+++.>++.<<+++++++++++++++.>.+++.------.--------.>+.>.");

Here we have a brainfuck interpreter. And the example program we want to partially evaluate does not require any input at all (in brainfuck , is the way you get input). So when we go to partially evaluate this, we will just get an answer. In this case, this program is actually brainfuck's "hello world". But what about a program with input?

function main() {
	return brainfuck(",>++[>+++[>++++[<<<+>>>-]<-]<-]<.", process.argv[2])
}

When we do our partial evaluation, we get the following:

function main(b) {
  let a;
  a: {
    a = process.argv[2];
    a = a === void 0 ? "" : a;
    if (0 < a.length) {
      a = a.charCodeAt(0);
      break a;
    }
    a = 0;
  }
  a = (a & 255) + 24 & 255;
  return String.fromCharCode(a);
}

What is this? A compiled brainfuck program! This is the first incredible fact: when you take an interpreter and partially evaluate it with a program, you get the compiled program out! Now this particular exact form is an artifact of how my partial evaluator works. You could imagine slightly different code. But the key is that what we've done is remove the interpreter completely.

The Projections#

What we've discovered here is the first of three so-called Futamura Projections. Our partial evaluator, when applied to an interpreter and given a program, can give us a compiled version of that program. Or to put it in pseudocode.

partial_eval(interpreter, prog) -> compiled_prog

Depending on your exposure to interpreters and compilers, this might seem miraculous or mundane. Writing an interpreter and writing a compiler can seem like significantly different undertakings. In the age of AI, perhaps less so, but I think even then many things still hold. It is quite easy to instrument an interpreter, quite a bit harder to do so for a compiler. Changing an interpreter to support new features is quite easy, less so for a compiler. But more than that, there are all sorts of things that can be thought of as interpreters, that we'd almost never write a compiler for.

function validate(schema, value) {
  switch (schema.type) {
    case "string":
      return typeof value === "string" &&
        (schema.minLength === undefined || value.length >= schema.minLength);
    case "number":
      return typeof value === "number" && Number.isFinite(value) &&
        (schema.min === undefined || value >= schema.min);
    case "boolean":
      return typeof value === "boolean";
    case "array":
      if (!Array.isArray(value)) return false;
      const length = value.length;
      for (let i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        if (i in value && !validate(schema.items, value[i])) return false;
      }
      return true;
    case "object":
      return value !== null && typeof value === "object" &&
        !Array.isArray(value) &&
        Object.keys(schema.properties).every(key =>
          Object.hasOwn(value, key) &&
          validate(schema.properties[key], value[key]));
    default:
      throw new Error("Unknown schema type: " + schema.type);
  }
}

const userSchema = {
  type: "object",
  properties: {
    name: { type: "string", minLength: 1 },
    age: { type: "number", min: 0 },
    tags: { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } }
  }
};

function validateUser(value) {
  return validate(userSchema, value);
}

Consider this simple schema setup. This is code that can easily be partially evaled into something where we have created specialized functions for our particular schema. While not the most crucial code, this can give us a 5x performance boost when our objects start getting more complicated. You may think that we should just hand-write those functions. Or hand-write a compiler for these schemas. But what about those schemas that exist only at runtime? Now we either need to compile those on the fly, or we have to keep both a compiler and interpreter. Having a way to partial eval lowers this burden quite a bit.

Mind Bending#

But if the Futamura projections stopped here, they would be exciting, but not quite the craziness they are. To understand how this can go further, we are going to take this a step beyond your raw intuition of what it means to partially evaluate something and give a different frame. We can think of partial evaluation as a process of "specializing" a program.

What exactly is specializing a program? Well, it is taking a program that is generic and making a version that instead works for a single program. Let's think about a simple pattern matcher program like an overly simplified regex.

function matches(pattern, text) {
  if (pattern.length === 0) {
    return text.length === 0;
  }

  const firstCharacterMatches =
    text.length > 0 && pattern[0] === text[0];
  const allowsRepetition = pattern[1] === "*";

  if (allowsRepetition) {
    const remainingPattern = pattern.slice(2);

    if (matches(remainingPattern, text)) {
      return true;
    }

    if (!firstCharacterMatches) {
      return false;
    }

    const remainingText = text.slice(1);
    return matches(pattern, remainingText);
  }

  if (!firstCharacterMatches) {
    return false;
  }

  const remainingPattern = pattern.slice(1);
  const remainingText = text.slice(1);
  return matches(remainingPattern, remainingText);
}

matches("a*b*c", "aaabbc");

This program is generic. It lets you match on many different patterns. That can be great if we need that flexibility. But if you don't have a bunch of patterns, it might be worth it to just make specialized code. Now, exactly what kind of specialized code? It might be that you only have this literal pattern; then you want to specialize very particularly.

function matchesAStarBStarC(text) {
  let i = 0;
  while (text[i] === "a") i++;
  while (text[i] === "b") i++;
  return text[i] === "c" && i + 1 === text.length;
}

matchesAStarBStarC("aaabbc");

Or you just have <x>*<y>*<z>* as a pattern.

function matchesXStarYStarZStar(x, y, z, text) {
  let i = 0;
  while (i < text.length && text[i] === x) i++;
  while (i < text.length && text[i] === y) i++;
  while (i < text.length && text[i] === z) i++;
  return i === text.length;
}

matchesXStarYStarZStar("a", "b", "c", "aaabbc");

For any bit of generic code, we can think of how to move our code to a more specialized form.

Specializing the Specializer#

Partial evaluation is a form of specialization that figures out what it should specialize on based on what input is static and what is dynamic. In many ways, a partial evaluator is a generic specializer. Given any program, we can make a specialized version of it for any input. What happens if we specialize an interpreter for a given input? We get back that interpreter for only exactly that one program. But what do we need then? Do we need all this generic dispatch? No, we know the full program. We don't need any operations we don't actually use. We can fully get rid of all the generic interpreter mechanism.

But if the specializer can specialize any program, can it specialize itself?

This leads us to the second Futamura projection. Put in our pseudo-code format, we get:

partial_eval(partial_eval, interpreter) -> compiler

Or, to put it in our specializer language, what if we make a special version of our generic specializer? What is it specialized for? A particular interpreter. Now we have a function that, given any program, will spit out newly specialized interpreters just for that program. Or, in Java speak, we have a specialized interpreter factory.

Let's see a real example of one of these compilers to make this concrete. Here is the interpreter we are going to specialize.

function interp(program, io) {
  var value = null;
  while (program.length > 0) {
    var instruction = program[0];

    if (instruction === "prompt") {
      value = io.prompt();
    } else if (instruction === "print") {
      io.print(value);
    } else {
      throw new Error("Unknown instruction: " + instruction);
    }

    program = program.slice(1);
  }
  return value;
}

When we apply our second projection, we get out the following compiler:

function compile(program) {
  const lines = codegen.buffer();
  const literalSource = codegen.literal(null).source;
  let remaining = program;
  let value = literalSource;

  while (remaining.length > 0) {
    const remainingItem = remaining[0];
    if (remainingItem === "prompt") {
      const ioReference = codegen.reference("io");
      const callSource = codegen.call(lines, ioReference, "prompt", []).source;
      remaining = remaining.slice(1);
      value = callSource;
      continue;
    }
    if (remainingItem === "print") {
      const ioReference2 = codegen.reference("io");
      const args = [codegen.reference(value)];
      codegen.call(lines, ioReference2, "print", args);
      remaining = remaining.slice(1);
      continue;
    }
    const text = "Unknown instruction: " + remainingItem;
    throw new Error(text);
  }

  const valueReference = codegen.reference(value);
  return codegen.finish(lines, valueReference);
}

And if we compile one of these very simple programs, we can see the output:

compile(["prompt", "print"])

// returns as a string
function run(io) {
	var v0 = io.prompt();
	var v1 = io.print(v0);
	return v0;
}

Now, of course, this is not a very interesting language. But hopefully you can see this general idea. Given an interpreter, we automatically derive a compiler! Pretty incredible.

The Third Projection#

But we can't stop at the second projection. We have to push on and get to the final mind-bending projection. If you apply our specializer to itself as input, you get a compiler generator.

partial_eval(partial_eval, partial_eval) -> compiler_generator

So now we have a generic function that will spit out compilers for any interpreter we give it!

Playing With It#

I have implemented a reasonable, but still very limited partial evaluator for JavaScript in Rust. I have taken it further to try to make it work quite well for a number of different interpreters and interpreter-like programs in JavaScript. I've also tried to get limited versions of the second and third projections working. Go play with it, see what works, what doesn't, file issues, or better, use some of your tokens to help me make more cases work.

But most of all, explore. This is such a rich space. Below are some papers, blogs, and projects about partial evaluation in some way, shape, or form. There has never been a better time to play with these kinds of crazy techniques for programming languages. Don't let what is practical stop you from exploring the cool, interesting aspects of programming.

  • weval: the WebAssembly partial evaluator
  • Compilation of JavaScript to Wasm, Part 3: Partial Evaluation — Chris Fallin

item.description:

LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team.

The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change?

According to the Financial Times, the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions.

Subscribe

KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised.

The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged.

From supporting accountants to conducting audits

Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow.

The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation.

The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts.

Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks.

KPMG plans to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively.

A challenge to the Big Four business model?

The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial.

Traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions.

For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information.

However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees.

Human judgement remains the final safeguard

The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism.

There are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used.

The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise.

For the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does.

item.description:
URL: https://www.wiz.io/blog/nginx-http2-rce-vulnerabilities, See on Hacker News

Executive Summary

  • Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.

  • NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server, it powers more than 225 million websites.

  • Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

  • The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.

  • We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.

  • We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.

Responsible disclosure timeline

  • October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.

  • November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.

  • November 16, 2026: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.

  • November 17, 2026: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.

  • November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.

Overview

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered  CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.

Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.

The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.

Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.

In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.

What is NGINX?

NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server, powering more than 225 million websites. It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.

NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.

The Vulnerabilities

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Tracking IDThe bugWhat an attacker can achieve
CVE-2026-123633HTTP/2 connection use-after-freeExecute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.
CVE-2026-123007HTTP/2 send_window integer underflowExecute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.

Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.

Impact

On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.

An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.

Coordinated disclosure

We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.

Mitigation and detection

Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available.

ProductCVE and first affected version or branchFixed releases
NGINX OSSCVE-2026-123633: 1.19.71.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline
NGINX PlusCVE-2026-123633: R33; 37.0.037.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1
NGINX OSSCVE-2026-123007: 1.9.51.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline
NGINX PlusCVE-2026-123007: R33; 37.0.037.0.8.1; 37.3.0.1

If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances:

  • Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives.

  • Test application compatibility, reload NGINX, and confirm the old workers have exited.

Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.

Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities.

Technical deep dive

CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable

NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.

We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:

ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1);

if (h2c->state.incomplete) {

    return;

}

When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing. However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.

Triggering the use-after-free

Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.

Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection(). When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.

Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.

From use-after-free to remote code execution

The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection.

This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow

Returning credit for unsent data

HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window.

When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:

h2c->send_window += window;

This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.

A bounds check that no longer works

The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update(), which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window)

The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.

From an invalid length to remote code execution

The invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.

When the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.

Exploitation

To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.

Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.

Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation.

Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.

How Can Wiz Help?

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Conclusion

With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.

As we saw with PHP2Shell, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.

The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.

Stay in touch

Hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

item.title: Poland says it thwarted false flag operation near border with Kaliningrad (352 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/russia-reportedly-planned-mass-casualty-090500574.html, See on Hacker News

Russian intelligence services reportedly planned to carry out a sabotage operation on Polish territory near the border with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast in late October or early November which they intended to be blamed on Ukraine.

Source: Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita, as cited by European Pravda

Details: The newspaper cited senior sources with ties to Poland's military and security services who are familiar with an operation carried out over the past two weeks to foil the Russian plot.

Rzeczpospolita said Warsaw had been warned of the planned operation by partner intelligence services, and Polish intelligence analysts had also identified signs of the threat.

"We had information about the specific sites that were to be attacked. The Russian plan envisaged mass casualties," one of the newspaper's sources said.

Drawing parallels with the Gleiwitz incident, a German false-flag operation carried out on 31 August 1939, another source said: "It was supposed to be something similar to Gleiwitz. Of course, those who crossed the border would most likely have been shot, or evidence that they had come from Ukraine would have been found on them. The aim was to stop aid to Ukraine."

Polish intelligence services took action after Russian intelligence officers responsible for coordinating sabotage operations appeared on the Russian side of the border. Such operations are mainly planned and coordinated by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU.

Police forces in areas bordering Russia were reinforced by officers from other parts of Poland in late October for this reason. Border Guard posts also received reinforcements, and additional Internal Security Agency officers were deployed to the area. Special forces held exercises in the Warmian-Masurian region, where Poland's Territorial Defence Forces had also held exercises earlier.

"The aim was deterrence, but also to ensure the ability to take pre-emptive action," a source familiar with the details said.

Rzeczpospolita asked Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland's Minister-Coordinator of Special Services, whether the Russians had planned to carry out a terrorist attack in Poland at a location where large numbers of people might have been present.

"I don't know the answer to that question – you'd have to ask the Russians, and they don't usually admit to planning such actions. Even if we have such information, we don't share it," he replied.

Siemoniak added, however: "If we took certain measures, it was because we considered the threat to be real.

In my opinion, all the measures taken in this case were appropriate. The available evidence indicated that the threat had been assessed as real," the minister said.

Background:

  •  In early November, a special operations headquarters was established at Poland's National Police Headquarters for an operation being conducted in the Warmian-Masurian and Podlaskie voivodeships. Security forces were preparing for possible acts of sabotage on the border with Kaliningrad Oblast. 

  •  On 3 November, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that "suspicious activity" had been detected overnight on the Polish-Russian border.

item.title: The x86 CPU: From 4004 to 486 (149 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://pikuma.com/blog/history-of-x86-4004-to-486, See on Hacker News

Why is x86 little-endian? Why are the registers called AX, BX, CX, and DX? Why do DOS programmers write addresses like A000:0000, and why does a modern PC still wake up pretending to be a chip from 1978? The answers are not in the datasheets. They are in the story of how each chip was born.

We already covered the main ideas behind Real Mode & Protected Mode in one of our previous posts. This article will build on those concepts and take a deeper look at the history and evolution of the x86 family of CPUs. But rather than simply looking at the innovations introduced with each new chip, we need to understand how the architecture accumulated over time, from its origins in the early 70s up until the launch of the 486.

Every time a new student starts learning x86 assembler with us, it's not rare to hear them complain that many aspects of the instruction set look arbitrary. An accumulator that some instructions insist on, a base register that is the only one allowed to point at memory, a parity flag nobody seems to use, and an addressing scheme that adds two 16-bit numbers together in a very strange way.

The majority of teaching resources out there will help you write your first lines of x86 code, assemble it, link it, and as proceed as soon as the output matches what you were expecting. I try to always explain the evolution of the x86 family of CPUs, so every aspect of our code makes a little bit more sense.

None of these things are arbitrary, of course. Each one is a decision someone made under pressure, usually to keep old software running on a new chip. If you want to really understand x86 (and especially if you want to program a 486 under DOS), the best place to start is not the 486 manual. It's the story.

Here is the family tree we're going to walk through:

Year Chip Width Addr. space What it added that still shows up in x86
197140044-bit4 KB prog. ROMIntel's first CPU, for a Busicom calculator
197280088-bit16 KBRegister set A, B, C, D, E, H, L; little-endian order and a parity flag, both inherited from the Datapoint 2200 terminal it was designed for
197480808-bit64 KB16-bit register pairs (BC, DE, HL), a real stack pointer, a separate 256-port I/O space with IN/OUT
197680858-bit64 KBOne 5 V supply; address and data multiplexed on the same pins to save pins
1978808616-bit1 MBSegmentation, a prefetch queue, 16-bit registers that contain the 8080's 8-bit ones
1979808816-bit inside, 8-bit bus1 MBThe cheaper version IBM chose for the 1981 PC
19828028616-bit16 MBProtected mode with segment descriptors and privilege rings
19858038632-bit4 GB32-bit registers, paging, virtual 8086 mode
19898048632-bit4 GBOn-chip cache and FPU, a 5-stage pipeline

A table like this makes the evolution look neat and planned. It wasn't. Between these rows there are cancelled projects, a customer who walked away from its own chip, a stopgap that was supposed to last a couple of years, a sales campaign, a keyboard controller wired into the address bus, and a lawsuit.

Let's travel back to 1969 and see how it all happened!

A Calculator Chip: The 4004

The story starts with a Japanese calculator company. In 1969, Busicom asked Intel (then a young memory company) to build a set of custom chips for a new printing calculator. Instead of designing many single-purpose chips, Intel's team proposed something more general: a small programmable processor that would run the calculator's logic from ROM.

Intel 4004

The result was the 4004, released on November 15, 1971, and designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. It had 2,300 transistors, ran at about 740 kHz, and could address 4 KB of program ROM.

Chip layout from the development phase of the Intel 4004 (source)

The most important line in the 4004's story is not technical, though. Busicom had paid for the design and owned the rights. When Busicom ran into financial trouble in 1971, Faggin convinced Intel's CEO Bob Noyce to lower the chip's price in exchange for Intel getting out of the exclusivity deal. Intel paid back Busicom's $60,000 development costs and won the right to sell the chip to anyone (outside the calculator market).

That deal is why "a microprocessor" became something Intel could sell, rather than a part buried inside one calculator.

The Terminal That Didn't Want Its CPU: The 8008

At almost the same time, a second customer walked through Intel's door. In late 1969, Computer Terminal Corporation (CTC, later called Datapoint) asked Intel to build a chip for a programmable terminal called the Datapoint 2200.

This detail matters a lot: Intel did not design the instruction set of this chip. CTC's engineers Victor Poor and Harry Pyle did. They had already built the Datapoint 2200's processor out of dozens of discrete TTL chips, and they wanted Intel to squeeze that same design onto one piece of silicon.

Datapoint 2200 programmable terminal

Intel was slow. Texas Instruments also tried to build the chip, but its samples were buggy and rejected. Meanwhile, CTC shipped the Datapoint 2200 in 1970 with its TTL processor anyway, and later moved on to a faster design. In the end, CTC voted to walk away from the project and leave the design to Intel instead of paying the $50,000 contract. Intel renamed it the 8008 and released it in April 1972 with 3,500 transistors and 16 KB of addressable memory.

So the ancestor of every x86 chip was designed by a terminal company, for a terminal, and then rejected by that terminal company. And two of the terminal's habits are still inside your PC today.

Why x86 is Little-Endian

The Datapoint 2200 processed numbers one bit at a time (a bit-serial design). If you're adding two numbers one bit at a time, you want to start with the lowest bit, because that's where the carry starts. So it made sense to store the lowest byte first in memory.

The 8008 copied the Datapoint's design, the 8080 kept compatibility with the 8008, and the 8086 kept compatibility with the 8080. Stephen Morse, the architect of the 8086, put it this way in his history of the early Intel processors:

"This inverted storage, which was to haunt all processors evolved from the 8008, was a result of compatibility with the Datapoint bit-serial processor."

That's why, on your 486 (and even in a more modern Core i9), this instruction:

mov DWORD ptr [buffer], 12345678h

...stores the bytes 78 56 34 12 in memory.

Why x86 Has a Parity Flag

The second habit is the parity flag (PF), which tells you if the result of the last operation had an even number of 1 bits. It's one of those flags that beginners look at and wonder who on earth needs it.

The answer is: a terminal does! Morse again: "This permits testing for transmission errors, an obviously useful function for a CRT terminal." Data arriving over a serial line often carried a parity bit, and the Datapoint needed a fast way to check it.

Fifty years later, PF is still bit 2 of the x86 FLAGS register.

The 8080 and the Birth of the PC Hobby

The 8008 was slow and awkward, so Intel designed a much better successor. The 8080 was released in April 1974, with Federico Faggin as its primary architect and Masatoshi Shima on the detailed design. It had about 4,500 transistors, ran at 2 MHz, and could address 64 KB of memory.

The 8080 was not binary compatible with the 8008, but it kept the same register set and the same "flavor." More importantly, it added several things you will recognize as an x86 programmer:

  • Register pairs: B and C could be used together as the 16-bit pair BC, and the same for DE and HL
  • The HL pair as the main way to point at memory (MOV A, M reads the byte at address HL)
  • A real 16-bit stack pointer
  • A separate I/O space with 256 ports, accessed with IN and OUT

That separate I/O space is the reason why, many years later, VGA registers live at "port 3C8h" instead of at a memory address.

MITS Altair 8800, powered by an Intel 8080

The 8080 powered the Altair 8800 and became the standard CPU for CP/M, the most popular operating system for small business computers in the late 70s. Suddenly, there was a lot of 8080 software out there.

And then Intel got some serious competition. Faggin and Shima left Intel and went to Zilog, where they built the Z80: a chip that could run 8080 machine code, but was faster, cheaper to build a computer around, and had more instructions. The Z80 started eating Intel's market.

The 8085: A Quiet Hint of What Was Coming

Intel's answer was the 8085, released in March 1976. The "5" in the name refers to its biggest selling point: it needed a single +5 V power supply, while the 8080 needed +5 V, -5 V, and +12 V.

To fit everything into a 40-pin package, the 8085 also multiplexed its bus: the same eight pins carried the low byte of the address first, and then the data. Remember this trick, because the 8086 uses it too.

There's a lovely footnote here: the 8085 had 12 new instructions, but Intel made a last-minute decision to document only 2 of them. The reason? To keep things simple for the next chip, which was already being designed. That chip was the 8086.

The Stopgap That Took Over the World: The 8086

In the mid 70s, Intel's big bet for the future was not the 8086. It was the iAPX 432, a very ambitious processor designed with object-oriented programming and high-level languages in mind. The 432 was late, and with the Z80 taking customers away, Intel needed something to sell in the meantime.

So, in May 1976, Intel started the 8086 project as a temporary product. Stephen Morse was the principal architect, Jim McKevitt and John Bayliss were the lead hardware engineers, and Bill Pohlman managed the project. The 8086 was released on June 8, 1978.

Intel 8086

The brief was clear: the new chip had to address more than 64 KB, do 16-bit arithmetic, and (this is the important part) make it easy for existing 8080 software to move over.

Source Compatibility, Not Binary Compatibility

The 8086 cannot run 8080 machine code. Instead, Intel aimed for source compatibility: you could take your 8080 assembly program and translate it, line by line, into 8086 assembly. Intel even shipped a translator called CONV86 (available from 1978) to do this automatically. Morse described the goal like this: "the 8080 register set and instruction set appear as logical subsets of the 8086 registers and instructions."

For that translation to work, every 8080 register needed an obvious home in the 8086. And this is where the 8086's register names come from:

How the 8080 registers map into the 8086

Here's a tiny 8080 routine and its 8086 translation side by side:

; 8080                     ; 8086
LXI  H, buffer             mov  bx, offset buffer   ; HL becomes BX
MOV  A, M                  mov  al, [bx]            ; A becomes AL
INX  H                     inc  bx
ADD  M                     add  al, [bx]

Now some of the "weird" things about x86 suddenly make sense:

  • AX is the accumulator because 8080's A became AL. That's why MUL, DIV, IN, and OUT insist on using it, and why many instructions have shorter encodings when they use AL/AX.
  • BX is the base register because the 8080's memory pointer HL became BX. That's why, in 16-bit code, BX is the only one of AX, BX, CX, DX that can point at memory.
  • CX is the count register (used by LOOP, REP, and shifts) and DX is the data register (used for I/O port numbers and the high half of 32-bit results).
  • The 8080's flags byte became the low byte of the 8086's FLAGS register, and the instructions LAHF and SAHF exist just to move that 8080-shaped byte in and out of AH.

Have you ever wondered why the 8086 numbers its registers in the order AX, CX, DX, BX (0, 1, 2, 3) inside instruction encodings, instead of the obvious A, B, C, D? It follows the 8080's order of register pairs: BC, DE, HL. Once A is placed first, BC becomes CX, DE becomes DX, and HL becomes BX.

And what does the "X" mean? According to Morse himself, nothing special. It was simply an arbitrary letter combining the "H" and "L" halves into one 16-bit register (as told to Vladimir Keleshev).

Segmentation: Reaching 1 MB with 16-bit Registers

The second big requirement was memory. Intel wanted 1 MB of address space, and that needs 20 address bits. But the 8086's registers were only 16 bits wide.

Morse's solution was segmentation. The chip has four segment registers (CS, DS, SS, and ES), and every memory access combines a segment with a 16-bit offset:

$$ \text{address} = \text{segment} \times 16 + \text{offset} $$

Multiplying by 16 is just a shift of 4 bits to the left. For example, if we want to write to pixel (160, 100) in VGA mode 13h, which lives at segment A000h:

mov  ax, 0A000h
mov  es, ax                       ; segment = A000h
mov  di, 320*100 + 160            ; offset  = 7DA0h
mov  byte ptr es:[di], 15         ; physical address = A0000h + 7DA0h = A7DA0h

The segment is shifted left by one hex digit, then the offset is added

Why 16 and not something bigger, like 256? Morse explained that with 8 bits of shift, "segments would be forced to start on 256-byte boundaries, resulting in excessive memory fragmentation."

Segmentation was cheap (a small adder in the chip) and it worked very well with the source-compatibility goal: an 8080 program expected a 64 KB world, so you could give it one segment and it would run unchanged, wherever in memory that segment happened to be.

But it also created a rule that haunted every DOS programmer for the next 15 years:

No single object can be bigger than 64 KB without doing arithmetic on segment registers yourself.

That rule is why C compilers for DOS had near, far, and huge pointers, and memory models with names like tiny, small, compact, and large. It's also why mode 13h is so beloved: 320 × 200 = 64,000 bytes, which fits in one segment!

Operation Crush and the 8088

The 8086 was not an instant hit. Motorola's 68000 and Zilog's Z8000 were more elegant 16-bit designs, and many engineers preferred them.

Intel's response was a sales campaign called Operation Crush, launched in a meeting in December 1979. Instead of selling the 8086 on raw specs, Intel sold it as a complete solution: development tools, support chips, documentation, and support. The goal was 2,000 "design wins" (products using the chip) in one year. They got nearly 2,500.

One of them was a small project inside IBM in Boca Raton.

A year after the 8086, Intel had released the 8088 (June 1, 1979). Internally it's the same 16-bit processor, but with an 8-bit external data bus. Every 16-bit memory access takes two bus cycles, so it's slower. But an 8-bit bus meant you could build the computer with cheap, plentiful support chips designed for the 8085. Intel also offered IBM a better price and could supply more units.

IBM Personal Computer (model 5150)

The IBM PC was launched on August 12, 1981, with an 8088 running at 4.77 MHz. That odd number comes from television: the PC used a 14.31818 MHz crystal (four times the NTSC color carrier, which the CGA video card needed), divided by 3.

IBM made one more decision that shaped the whole industry: it required a second source for the CPU, so it would never depend on a single supplier. That led to a 10-year technology exchange agreement between Intel and AMD, first signed in October 1981 and formally executed in February 1982. Keep that agreement in mind, because it comes back with the 386.

The famous "640 KB limit" is not a limit of the CPU. The 8088 could address 1 MB. It was IBM who placed video memory at address A0000h (that's 640 KB) and the BIOS ROM at the top of memory, leaving 640 KB of conventional memory for DOS and its programs.

The "temporary" 8086 family was now inside the machine that would define personal computing. From this point on, every new Intel chip had to run software written for the IBM PC. Compatibility was no longer a nice-to-have.

The 286: Protection Nobody Could Use

The 80286 was released on February 1, 1982, with 134,000 transistors. IBM used it in the PC/AT in 1984, running at 6 MHz.

The 286 was designed for multitasking operating systems. Its new protected mode changed what a segment register means: instead of holding a paragraph number, it holds a selector, an index into a table of descriptors. Each descriptor says where a segment starts (anywhere in 16 MB of memory), how big it is, and who is allowed to use it. The chip checks every memory access against those rules, and runs code in one of four privilege "rings."

On paper, this was fantastic. In practice, it had three problems:

  • Segments were still limited to 64 KB.
  • DOS programs routinely did arithmetic on segment values (adding 1 to a segment means "16 bytes further"). In protected mode, that produces a random selector and a crash.
  • And the biggest one: once you switched to protected mode, you couldn't switch back.

Entering protected mode was as simple as setting one bit:

smsw ax          ; read the Machine Status Word
or   ax, 1       ; set the PE (Protection Enable) bit
lmsw ax          ; ...and there's no instruction to undo this

But DOS and the BIOS only worked in real mode. So how did the PC/AT get back? IBM built a hack into the motherboard: the program wrote a "shutdown code" into the CMOS memory, then asked the keyboard controller to pulse the CPU's reset line. The CPU rebooted, the BIOS noticed the shutdown code, and jumped back into the program, now in real mode. It worked, but it was painfully slow.

Bill Gates famously called the 286 "brain-damaged," mainly because it couldn't run several DOS programs side by side under a protected-mode operating system. Most 286 machines spent their lives running DOS in real mode, as a very fast 8086.

The A20 Gate

The 286 created another, stranger problem. On the 8086, the highest address you can form is FFFF:FFFF, which is 10FFEFh. That needs 21 bits, but the 8086 only has 20 address lines, so the top bit is lost and the address wraps around to the bottom of memory.

The same address on an 8086 and on a 286

Some software depended on that wraparound. DOS's CP/M-style CALL 5 entry point relied on it to reach code at physical address C0h, and programs built with IBM/Microsoft Pascal used it as a space-saving trick. The 286 has 24 address lines, so it does not wrap, and those programs broke.

IBM's fix was to put a logic gate on address line 20 (A20), controlled by... a spare pin on the 8042 keyboard controller. With the gate closed, the PC/AT wraps at 1 MB like an 8086. With it open, real-mode code can reach the High Memory Area: 65,520 bytes just above 1 MB, which is where DOS=HIGH loads DOS.

This hack lived much longer than anyone expected:

Later chipsets added a faster "A20" switch at port 92h, the 486 added an A20M# pin to the CPU itself, and according to Intel's manuals, Intel only stopped supporting the A20 gate with the Haswell processors (2013). Source.

The 286 also had an undocumented instruction called LOADALL that could load the CPU's hidden segment caches directly, which tools like HIMEM.SYS used to reach extended memory without the slow reset trip. Hidden segment caches will come back very soon.

The 386: Intel Goes Alone

The 80386 was introduced as samples in October 1985, with mass production starting in June 1986. It had 275,000 transistors, and its chief architect was John Crawford (Pat Gelsinger, years later Intel's CEO, also worked on the project).

Intel 80386

The 386 fixed the 286's problems one by one:

  • 32-bit registers: EAX, EBX, ECX... (the "E" means extended), with AX and AL still living inside them.
  • 4 GB segments: set every segment to start at 0 with a 4 GB limit and segmentation effectively disappears. This "flat model" is what DOS extenders like DOS/4GW (used by Doom) gave to C programmers.
  • Paging: memory split into 4 KB pages with a two-level page table, which made real virtual memory possible.
  • Virtual 8086 mode: a protected-mode task that behaves like an 8086. This is how EMM386 and Windows ran DOS programs safely, each believing it owned the machine.
  • A way back: clearing the PE bit in CR0 returns to real mode. No keyboard controller needed!
mov  eax, cr0
and  al, 0FEh    ; clear PE
mov  cr0, eax    ; back in real mode, no reset required

Combining the way back with those hidden segment caches gave demo coders a favorite trick: unreal mode. You enter protected mode, load a segment register with a 4 GB limit, and return to real mode without reloading it. The CPU keeps using the cached 4 GB limit, so your real-mode program (with DOS still working!) can read and write all of memory using 32-bit offsets.

How did 32 bits fit into an instruction set designed for 16? Intel didn't add new opcodes for 32-bit operations. Instead, it added a bit to each code segment that sets the default size, plus two prefix bytes (66h for operand size and 67h for address size) that flip it for a single instruction. That's why a DOS program running in real mode on a 386 can still use EAX: the assembler simply adds a 66h prefix in front of the instruction.

The Business Decision

The 386's biggest story was not technical. Intel decided that the 386 would be single-source. As early as 1984, Intel had decided to stop cooperating with AMD, and it delayed and eventually refused to hand over the 386's technical details. AMD invoked arbitration in 1987, Intel cancelled the 1982 agreement, and the fight went on for years. AMD released its own Am386 in March 1991 (and sold one million of them by October of that year), and in 1994 the Supreme Court of California sided with AMD.

Then something happened that would have been unthinkable a few years before: IBM was not first. The Compaq Deskpro 386 shipped in September 1986, the first time a fundamental part of the IBM PC standard was moved forward by a company other than IBM.

Compaq Deskpro 386

And one more fun detail: some early 386 chips had a bug in 32-bit multiplication. Intel marked the affected chips with "16 BIT S/W ONLY", which was fine at the time because almost all software was still 16-bit anyway!

The 486: Same Instructions, New Engine

The 486 was announced at Spring Comdex on April 10, 1989, and it was the first x86 chip with more than one million transistors (about 1.2 million).

Intel 486

Here's the interesting part: the 486 added almost nothing to the architecture. A few instructions, like BSWAP, XADD, and CMPXCHG, and some control bits. What changed was the engine underneath:

  • An 8 KB on-chip cache (16 KB on the later DX4)
  • The floating-point unit integrated on the same chip
  • A tightly pipelined five-stage design, where simple instructions finally finished in a single clock

Intel kept spinning variants: the 486SX (September 1991) with the FPU disabled, the clock-doubled DX2 (March 1992) that ran the core twice as fast as the motherboard, and the clock-tripled DX4 (March 1994).

For assembly programmers, the pipeline changed the rules of optimization. On the 8086, every instruction ran through microcode, and the "clever" complex instructions were often the fastest way to do things. On the 486, simple instructions became fast, and the old clever ones became the slow ones. The classic example is LOOP:

Code 8086 (clocks) 486 (clocks)
loop label (taken)177
dec cx + jnz label (taken)2 + 16 = 181 + 3 = 4

On an 8086, LOOP was the fast way to write a loop. On a 486, it's almost twice as slow as the "naive" version. If you read Michael Abrash's Graphics Programming Black Book, you'll see this shift everywhere: forget the microcoded tricks, use simple instructions, and keep your data inside the cache.

And Then It Got a Name

So why isn't the next chip called the 586? Because in 1991 Intel lost a trademark dispute over the name "386," when a judge ruled that a number was generic and could not be trademarked. AMD could call its chips "386" and "486" too.

Intel hired a branding agency and came up with a name instead of a number. The Pentium (from the Greek word for "five") was introduced on March 22, 1993. A few years later it would get those famous "with MMX technology" stickers, but that's another story.

Conclusion

Hopefully, by now, you can look at an x86 instruction set reference and see it as a geological record. Every layer was laid down by a specific event:

The quirk Where it came from
Little-endian byte orderThe bit-serial Datapoint 2200 terminal (1970)
The parity flagChecking transmission errors on a CRT terminal
AX as the accumulator, BX as the only memory pointer of the fourThe 8080's A and HL, mapped for source compatibility (1978)
IN/OUT and a separate port spaceThe 8080 (1974)
Segment:offset addresses and the 64 KB limitReaching 1 MB cheaply with 16-bit registers (1978)
The 640 KB limitIBM's memory map for the PC (1981)
The A20 gateKeeping wraparound-dependent DOS software alive on the PC/AT (1984)
Starting every PC in real modeEvery chip since the 8086 must boot like an 8086

The pattern is always the same. A chip is designed quickly, often as a stopgap, with one very practical goal in mind. Software starts to depend on its exact behavior (including its accidents). And from that moment on, every future chip has to carry that behavior forward, emulate it, or work around it with a hack.

That's the real lesson of x86 history: the architecture wasn't designed, it accumulated. And once you know the story, the quirks stop being things you memorize and start being things you can explain.

If you're curious to dig deeper, Stephen Morse's "Intel Microprocessors: 8008 to 8086" is a great read straight from the architect, and Ken Shirriff's blog has amazing die-level reverse engineering of the 8086.

And that's it for our trip from a calculator chip to the 486. If you have any suggestions for this article, you can yell at me on Twitter. Also, remember to visit the courses page to access my lectures on retro programming.
